props.title: Myra Breckinridge

sections.content: **Myra Breckinridge** (1970) stands as one of Hollywood's most notorious catastrophes - a surreal, hypersexual satire that nearly destroyed 20th Century Fox. Based on Gore Vidal's controversial novel, the film stars Raquel Welch as a transgender woman who aims to destroy the American male. Director Michael Sarne created a bizarre mashup of Old Hollywood clips, sexual politics, and experimental filmmaking that baffled audiences. The film's troubled production included Mae West's return to cinema after 27 years, Rex Reed's acting debut, and constant battles between cast members. Like **Beyond the Valley of the Dolls** (1970), it represents a moment when major studios briefly embraced counterculture excess. movies.title: Myra Breckinridge
movies.slug: Raquel Welch stars in this controversial adaptation about a transgender woman's mission to upend masculinity and Hollywood

sections.content: The film's legacy lies in its audacious failure to merge Old Hollywood with New Hollywood sensibilities. Sarne intercuts classic film clips from the Fox library as ironic commentary, prefiguring the postmodern approach of **Dead Men Don't Wear Plaid** (1982). The casting of film critic Rex Reed as Myra pre-transition was a meta-textual experiment that backfired spectacularly. Meanwhile, Mae West's presence as a talent agent represents the dying gasp of Classical Hollywood trying to stay relevant in the counterculture era.

While critically reviled, **Myra Breckinridge** pioneered transgender representation in mainstream cinema, however problematically. Its influence can be traced through films like **The World According to Garp** (1982), **The Crying Game** (1992), and Hedwig and the Angry Inch (2001). The film's examination of gender fluidity and Hollywood power structures, though heavy-handed, predicted contemporary discussions of gender identity in media. movies.slug: Groundbreaking musical about a genderqueer rock singer

sections.content: The film's spectacular failure marked the end of an era when studios would gamble on transgressive counterculture material. While directors like John Waters continued pushing boundaries independently with films like **Pink Flamingos** (1972), major studios retreated to safer territory. Yet **Myra Breckinridge**'s mashup aesthetic and media critique influenced later works like **Natural Born Killers** (1994) and **Velvet Goldmine** (1998).
